cards.back: The study of inherited characteristics that lie outside of the genome in organisms (from the word epi, meaning “outside” or “above,” originally from the Greek).
The study of DNA-based inherited characteristics in organisms.
A molecule consisting of DNA and histones; it is the primary constituent of a chromosome. When a chromosome is uncoiled, it is referred to as chromatin.
A tightly coiled macromolecule of DNA and its associated proteins.
A protein found in six different forms; four types form a core around which double-helix DNA winds to form chromatin, compacting DNA to fit inside the nucleus.
The fundamental unit of chromatin: two copies of each of the four core histones with 146 base pairs of DNA wrapped around them.
A double-stranded chain of nucleotides that carries a cell’s genetic information and is capable of self-replication and RNA synthesis.
A chemical compound consisting of a sugar, one phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine, and thymine.
Pairs of nucleotides adenine-thymine and cytosine-guanine that join by hydrogen bonding to form DNA’s double helix.
A single-stranded chain of nucleotides (one form of RNA) that acts as a messenger between DNA and the cell’s protein synthesis machinery.
The enzymatic copying process by which DNA produces a complementary copy of RNA.
The process by which a complete messenger RNA molecule serves as a template for the biosynthesis of a specific protein.

cards.front: Why enzymes have difficulty “reading” DNA in a coiled nucleosome
cards.back: In a nucleosome, DNA is wound onto histone proteins and nucleosomes are themselves coiled; the winding, twisting, and coiling make it essentially impossible for transcription enzymes to read a complete gene sequence.

cards.front: How methyl tags help chromatin uncoil
cards.back: When methyl groups attach to particular sites on tightly coiled chromatin, specific nucleosomes uncoil, revealing segments of base pairs (genes) so messenger RNA can be transcribed.

cards.front: methyl groups as an epigenetic factor
cards.back: Methyl groups originate outside the nucleus, pass through the nuclear membrane, and attach to activation sites on histones; this can cause affected chromatin to unravel and enable transcription.

cards.front: What if methyl groups stayed attached forever (kept chromatin continuously open)?
cards.back: There could be overproduction of a particular compound synthesized by that stretch of DNA; this overproduction might be related to cancer-like processes.
Coiling makes DNA’s nucleotide sequence hard to read, and in the tightly coiled state chromosomes are inactive—no transcription (or protein synthesis) can take place.
